summary: This informational memo specifies how ATM-attached hosts can set up direct IP over ATM connections on application request, for the exclusive use of that application.

plainLanguage.summary: An app asking for its own private express lane through the network.

subtitle: Applications request dedicated network connections with guaranteed service quality.

tldr.problem: Applications need to send data with guaranteed quality of service, but standard IP protocols do not provide this guarantee.
tldr.mechanism: AREQUIPA allows applications to request direct ATM connections with specific quality-of-service parameters, then use standard IP protocols over these dedicated links.
tldr.outcome: Only traffic from the requesting application uses the dedicated connection, ensuring predictable performance without rewriting transport protocols.

today: RFC 2170 is an Informational RFC from 1997 and has not been obsoleted. While AREQUIPA was implemented and tested, it did not become a widely deployed standard. IP over ATM was eventually superseded by other networking technologies, but the concepts remain relevant to understanding QoS in networks.

sections.title: The Need for Guaranteed Quality
sections.content:
AREQUIPA (Application REQuested IP over ATM) lets applications set up direct connections through an ATM network with guaranteed quality of service. The RFC solves a straightforward problem: when two applications on ATM-connected hosts need to exchange data reliably with specific performance guarantees—like latency or bandwidth—they lack a way to ask the network for those guarantees without bypassing IP entirely.

ATM networks are built to provide quality of service. They can guarantee bandwidth, delay and loss rates. But to use these features, applications traditionally had to abandon the standard IP protocol suite and implement their own communication protocols. AREQUIPA lets applications have both: they request a dedicated ATM connection with QoS parameters, and then use familiar, standard IP protocols like TCP or UDP over that connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally all apps share the network like cars on a highway. AREQUIPA lets an app ask for its own dedicated lane with a speed guarantee, then use it like a normal road.

sections.title: How the System Works
sections.content:
AREQUIPA introduces three API functions that applications call to manage dedicated connections: Arequipa_preset, Arequipa_expect, and Arequipa_close.

When application A1 on host H1 wants a dedicated connection to application A2 on host H2: First, both applications exchange information using standard IP—the receiving host's ATM address and the application endpoints (protocol and port). Next, A2 calls Arequipa_expect to signal readiness to accept an incoming dedicated connection. A1 calls Arequipa_preset to request an ATM connection to H2 with specified QoS parameters (like bandwidth and delay bounds). As soon as A1 sends data through its socket, the ATM connection is established. From that point forward, all traffic between A1 and A2 flows through the dedicated connection with the promised QoS.

A special identifier marks Arequipa connections at setup time, so hosts can distinguish them from normal IP over ATM traffic and reject unsolicited connections.
sections.plainLanguage: App A says "I want a fast lane to app B with these requirements." App B says "OK, I'm ready." When A sends the first message, the lane opens and stays open for their conversation.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Approaches
sections.content:
AREQUIPA works differently with IPv4 and IPv6 because of their different designs.

With IPv4, the system modifies the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) layer to track not just host-to-host mappings, but host-and-endpoint-to-host mappings. This allows one ATM connection per application pair. When setting up the connection, the sending host presets its ARP cache with the ATM address. When data arrives on an incoming dedicated connection, the receiving host identifies which application should use it and associates that socket with the connection.

With IPv6, the system exploits the Flow Label field in the IPv6 header. Each application flow is assigned a unique flow label, and destination caches hold entries for destination-address-and-flow-label pairs. The connection is associated with specific flow labels so only traffic from the intended applications uses it. This approach also extends the neighbor cache to allow reachability across the logical LIS (Link Interface Segment) boundary when a direct ATM connection exists.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 looks up the receiving app's mailbox number. IPv6 puts a special label on the message that only the right app recognizes.

sections.title: Web Browsing with QoS
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates Arequipa with HTTP: a web browser and server can use it to deliver multimedia documents with guaranteed quality. Browsers and servers extend HTTP headers to include ATM address and port information. When a browser requests a document marked with QoS metadata, it includes its ATM address in the request. The server checks whether the document needs QoS. If it does, the server opens an Arequipa connection to the browser's ATM address and transmits the file over it. The browser can first fetch just the header to see if the document needs QoS, then decide whether to request it with the full connection.

This scheme does not violate HTML or HTTP standards; it uses their built-in extension mechanisms, so non-Arequipa servers and browsers interoperate seamlessly.
sections.plainLanguage: A browser asks for a video and says "I can handle a fast lane." The server checks if that video needs one. If yes, it opens the fast lane and sends the video.

sections.title: Security and Firewall Implications
sections.content:
The main security risk is that Arequipa could bypass IP firewalls. A firewall controls which hosts can talk to each other by examining IP-level traffic. If internal hosts have direct ATM connectivity to the outside and can use Arequipa, they could establish connections that the firewall never sees.

The RFC addresses this through application proxies on the firewall. A proxy server (such as an HTTP proxy for the Web) runs on the firewall and mediates all Arequipa connections, examining and controlling traffic as it would any other connection. This preserves security while allowing internal hosts to benefit from QoS guarantees when talking through the proxy.

The system is safe because hosts can easily identify unsolicited Arequipa connection attempts by looking at the special BHLI (Broadband High Layer Identifier) marker in the setup message, and they can refuse connections that were not expected.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall is a bouncer at the door. Arequipa could sneak people in through a back door, but a proxy bouncer can still check everyone.
